en: At twelve he conquered a royal camp
And rode against a realm with its own court;
His fame spread across the world
And was entered in the chronicle
Of the khan of Kakan city.
He tended white stallions and gathered steeds,
Swiftly assembled valiant men,
And slaughtered ninety beasts for his feast.
A saint unlike ordinary men.
Go slaughter the gray beast,
And at the funeral feast, my orphan,
Eat until you are fully satisfied,
Then lay him in a place of honor.
Remember these solemn words;
My hero, my son, heed my counsel.
Your grandmother Kanykey
Was a great and holy woman;
That we were parted from the saint
Was a fate ordained by God.
Weeping and grieving in disgrace,
My darling, we were left behind,
Torn away from our motherland,
From my black-walled city with its gates,
From my village pitched upon the river terrace,
From the homeland that sustained me,
And from the angelic purity
Of my heroic mother.
I wailed aloud in grief,
And while my frail life yet clung sweetly,
I was parted from my true mother.
I screamed and wept till the pasture rang,
Enduring disgrace and bondage.
They dealt me a cruel fate
And slashed my breast open.
My two eyes rolled wildly,
My arms and legs hung limp;
Your fierce mother was bound,
And my two eyes wept a pasture of tears.
My blood drained away as I choked,
My poor coat was torn apart.
As I screamed in grief,
I was parted from my towering protector.
While I suffered plunder,
They cut down my banner with swords,
Hewed down my fruit with axes,
Trampled my living body underfoot,
Struck me heedless of my fury,
And reduced my days to a mere handful.
No hero could withstand that blade,
Nor could any man equal it;
Its steel nature was plain to see,
And two foes who faced it were cleft apart.
When enemies came face-to-face with it,
Their blood was spilled.
Know that such was Zulpukor:
When it unleashed tumult,
Its very blade became invisible,
While the hostile enemy’s coats and robes
Were taken away as plunder.
Upon the broad ridges of Talas,
The keen steel blade was left behind
In the hands of accursed Kanchoro.
Go gather and bring back your inheritance;
Say, “These are the possessions left by my father,”
And demand them from that treacherous dog.
If he will not heed your words,
If he refuses what you are to receive,
Come and tell wretched me,
“Mother, he refused to give it,”
And return without trading insults.
If you have the strength, go
To your aged grandsire Bakai,
And saying, “You are my inherited legacy,”
Bring your poor aged grandsire
Back here with you.
If by chance he has died,
If he has suddenly left this world,
If your grandsire has passed away,
Your elder, the hero Bakai,
Bend him gently, holding him at the waist,
And load him upon the gray beast.
If the chance is yours,
If you find a solitary place,
Choose a fitting spot and dig his grave,
Dedicate and slaughter the gray beast,
And with your own hands
Mark your grandsire’s grave and lay him there.
Your grandsire, the aged Bakai—
I drew it from its sheath.
When they pressed hard upon me,
When those accursed Jediger
Came surging furiously,
Shattering all my fortune,
Setting all I had aflame,
I took the keen Albar sword in hand.
Because of all that had befallen,
Because of your ill-fated mother,
A hundred Jediger champions
I struck down wounded.
The black-hearted Kanchoro,
That wicked black devil—
Curse my womanhood!
I failed and struck awry.
My bright eyes dimmed and wandered,
And from the mother who cherished me
I was left alive,
Torn away in disgrace.
The flesh of my right side
Was split apart by a bullet,
Twelve torments and a thousand cruelties
Loomed close above my head.
Sobbing and weeping in grief,
Through unheard-of shame and turmoil,
I was parted from my mother.
I did not spill your blood;
I still bore an uncertain child,
And so I could not bring myself
To take your accursed life.
Wailing shrilly in sorrow,
I was parted from the mother
Who sat cherishing me.
My heart burned and my blood drained,
And all strength left wretched me.
Curse my womanhood!
I have no mountain-high stronghold,
I suffered bitterly—the world is filth.
Curse my womanhood!
I have no strength left to fight.
When I screamed, none heard my voice;
When my true hero was slain,
When my blessed one wrought slaughter,
When they destroyed my gray-maned lord,
They tore away the noble woman,
From the hands of your wretched mother—
My mother, sacred as Mecca.
Though I pleaded, they heeded no word.
The days had shriveled me to a handful;
I embraced and kissed my darling,
Breathed once the scent of her breast—
Your venerable white-haired mother.
I tore my hair until it thinned;
Blood streaming from both my eyes
Flowed down over my breast.
I shrieked aloud in grief,
Parted from my own true mother.
As the vile ones beat me,
And subjected me to this disgrace,
I wished to sink into the earth, but it was hard;
I wished to die, but life was sweet.
They caused my darling bitter pain,
They ground me utterly to dust,
And dragged my mother away—
My generous venerable mother,
My broad-hearted dear one.
‘How can I remain alive?’ I cried.
‘From this day on, oh Mother,
Whom shall I hold sacred?’ I cried.
I turned my face toward death
And tore out my disheveled hair.
Because of all that had befallen,
Because of my dear mother,
I raised a piercing cry,
Not sparing my fly-sized soul.
‘Let me depart for the true world;
For my venerable white-haired mother,
I would gladly die contending.’
For six thousand camels and a thousand colts,
The keen Albar sword that was commissioned—
My mother entrusted it to you!
If you bring it back to me,
Bring my venerable white-haired mother
And let my eyes behold her.
Let me gaze upon her face,
Breathe once the scent of her breast,
And only then let me die!
My black crag no goose can circle,
My great mountain left by the departed,
Light of my seeing eyes,
Strength of my heart,
My only son, fare safely.
Your mother has no strength left.
Go in safety and return unharmed;
Do not leave your poor, wretched mother
Longing—come back quickly.
Go safely and return sound.
My orphaned son, if only
Once within seven days
I may safely see your face.
Saying, “My cherished orphan will return,”
I shall grieve for six days;
But if you do not come within six days,
If I do not see your radiant face,
I shall die before death comes.’
Moon-like Aichürök,
For the son she bore at death’s door,
Let her thoughts scatter far and wide.
Amid universal anguish and hardship,
Behold the plight of her only son.
Her heart was deeply troubled,
And tears poured from her eyes.
As though her son would never return,
Aichürök grieved,
Though he was merely setting forth
Upon a campaign.
So great was the poor woman’s anguish,
As though they would never meet again.
The woman screamed and shrieked,
Unable to bear it, she wailed.
There is no end to my misery.
The one who unleashed volleys of fire,
Who rescued us from calamity
More terrible than any battle cry—
My noble son is not here.
The support on which I relied,
The one in whom I placed my hopes,
My valiant son, is not there.
My heart burns; I have no courage left.
The enemy has torn away my wing;
My heart burns beneath the vast blue sky.
Had you been there then, my son,
Would they not have spared my blood?
Would they not have left my herds unscattered?
Would the raging Jediger
Not have spared my life?
Across the lower valley of Talas,
Would they have dared draw their boundary?
Would you not have faced them in battle
And crushed those evildoers?
Yesterday, when the enemy surrounded us,
When our people were left helpless
And suffered bitter torment,
I failed to do what was right—
Curse my womanhood!
I let them seize my livestock,
And let my life become their spoil.
I let them cut down my silken banner,
And let them drag away
The mother granted me by fortune.
If you encounter my mother,
Go and exchange greetings with her;
To be my strength and comfort,
Bring your noble, blessed mother
Back this way with you.
Let my eyes behold her;
Bring me the one I revere above all people—
My son, bring her back to me.
If you abandon her, shame will follow.
My heroic son, heed my words:
If one perishes, does not the black earth
Receive the whole world?
Do not grieve, Mother;
Will the descendant of a heroic khan
Rest before finding his people?
Would God strike down a warrior thus,
Leaving him unable to find his people?
The goshawk flies to its own land;
